abstract: Biofilms are spatially structured communities in which local microenvironments drive physiological differentiation, yet mapping gene expression inside intact three-dimensional biofilms remains challenging. Bacterial spatial transcriptomics methods typically rely on tiled probe sets, sequential hybridization rounds, or signal amplification. Here, we show that a single short, directly labelled peptide nucleic acid (PNA) probe per target is sufficient to quantify bacterial mRNA in situ without amplification. With all probes designed for a common hybridization condition, a transcript panel is resolved in one hybridization on a standard confocal microscope, in unmodified cells while preserving biofilm architecture. Benchmarked against the biphasic cycle of Legionella pneumophila, multiplex mRNA PNA-FISH recovers the expected transcriptional switch and agrees quantitatively with RT-qPCR in planktonic and biofilm populations. In flow-cell biofilms, it shows that sessile populations do not recapitulate the planktonic program and that transcriptional differences follow cellular aggregation state rather than depth.
